item.text: {"chapter_id":"8B","answers":[{"question_id":"8B.1","answer":"Tshisekedi revealed a mostly explicit, multi-component program: security and restoration of state authority; regional diplomacy and withdrawal of M23; elections; economic independence, diversification, macroeconomic stability, free education and health care; and territorial development through PDL-145T. These aims appeared in the official presidential program, campaign statements, State of the Nation address, security meetings, and monitoring roadmaps, making them sufficiently clear to test, although some commitments remained broad, rhetorical, or internally unresolved, particularly the relationship between military coercion and dialogue. Evidence of program clarity includes the 20-pillar presidential program and its supervised preparation (BATCH-0013-E007), dated economic and security commitments (BATCH-0006-E003; BATCH-0007-E006; BATCH-0007-E008; BATCH-0009-E009), and the CPVS roadmap and milestones (BATCH-0020-E011; BATCH-0020-E014). Qualifying evidence is that research describes the speeches as also serving authority-legitimation and mobilization, so rhetoric cannot by itself establish sincere or operational priorities (BATCH-0012-R09-E001; BATCH-0012-R09-E002).","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0013-E007","BATCH-0006-E003","BATCH-0007-E006","BATCH-0007-E008","BATCH-0009-E009","BATCH-0020-E011","BATCH-0020-E014"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0012-R09-E001","BATCH-0012-R09-E002","BATCH-0013-E004","BATCH-0027-E010"],"limitations_and_gaps":["The index provides limited detailed timetables and baseline targets for the full portfolio.","Many program claims come from presidential or government sources and are not independent evidence of priority sincerity."]},{"question_id":"8B.2","answer":"The ruler translated important parts of the program into laws, budgets, institutions, appointments, directives, and implementation machinery within presidential authority. Examples include PDL-145T’s financing, implementing agencies, construction targets, and monitoring structure; free-education and health-care measures; electoral-security instructions; judicial and anti-corruption institutions; security-sector and disarmament planning; and macroeconomic directives. The strongest evidence concerns formal operationalization rather than completed delivery: PDL-145T had planned financing, agencies, contracts, and works underway (BATCH-0008-E010; BATCH-0023-E001; BATCH-0023-E002), the CPVS tracked commitments (BATCH-0020-E011; BATCH-0020-E014), and formal laws, ordinances, judicial appointments, budget rules, and revenue instruments were adopted (BATCH-0009-E004; BATCH-0015-E006; BATCH-0015-E009; BATCH-0015-E010; BATCH-0029-E003; BATCH-0029-E004). The adverse qualification is that implementation was often dependent on ministers, donors, UN agencies, and regional actors, and several formal mechanisms lacked verified execution or results (BATCH-0014-E002; BATCH-0017-E005; BATCH-0016-E008).","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0008-E010","BATCH-0023-E001","BATCH-0023-E002","BATCH-0020-E011","BATCH-0020-E014","BATCH-0009-E004","BATCH-0015-E006","BATCH-0015-E009","BATCH-0015-E010","BATCH-0029-E003","BATCH-0029-E004"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0014-E002","BATCH-0017-E005","BATCH-0016-E008","BATCH-0013-E004","BATCH-0024-E003"],"limitations_and_gaps":["The candidate index contains little ruler-attributed evidence of final enforcement quality for many laws and budget instruments.","Formal acts do not establish that Tshisekedi personally controlled subordinate implementation."]},{"question_id":"8B.3","answer":"Mobilization was substantial but uneven. Tshisekedi used the presidency, cabinet, CPVS, provincial conferences, security services, FARDC, regional forces, and implementing agencies to pursue development, election, macroeconomic, and security priorities. PDL-145T mobilized state agencies, contractors, financing, and planned infrastructure across many territories (BATCH-0023-E001; BATCH-0023-E002; BATCH-0019-E009); the CPVS and governors’ conference created monitoring and coordination channels (BATCH-0020-E014; BATCH-0006-E007); and security meetings and military directives aligned FARDC, MONUSCO, EAC, and government institutions around eastern operations (BATCH-0021-E001; BATCH-0021-E003; BATCH-0019-E010). However, reliance on international financing, MONUSCO, EAC forces, humanitarian agencies, and allied armed groups limits attribution, while the EAC mandate ended after failing to produce expected results and the conflict continued (BATCH-0011-E016; BATCH-0011-E017; BATCH-0027-E006).","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0023-E001","BATCH-0023-E002","BATCH-0019-E009","BATCH-0020-E014","BATCH-0006-E007","BATCH-0021-E001","BATCH-0021-E003","BATCH-0019-E010"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0011-E016","BATCH-0011-E017","BATCH-0027-E006","BATCH-0014-E003","BATCH-0026-E005"],"limitations_and_gaps":["Administrative records show mobilization and planned deployment more clearly than delivered outputs.","The index does not provide a consolidated execution account for state spending, personnel, or regional reach."]},{"question_id":"8B.4","answer":"Tshisekedi actively appointed, reshuffled, and empowered personnel across the cabinet, military, judiciary, public enterprises, and regulatory institutions. The March cabinet reshuffle assigned defense, interior, economy, regional integration, justice, finance, planning, infrastructure, health, and education portfolios (BATCH-0009-E003); judicial ordinances promoted, removed, retired, and reassigned judges and prosecutors (BATCH-0015-E006; BATCH-0019-E006); and public-enterprise and regulatory appointments covered mining, statistics, agriculture, transport, employment, disaster management, and state firms (BATCH-0005-E004; BATCH-0008-E014). These choices show personnel control and attempts at institutional renewal, but the index does not reliably demonstrate competence, selection criteria, retention decisions, or performance. Adverse evidence includes appointments of inadequately vetted or politically connected security actors and the continued use of forces implicated in abuses (BATCH-0010-E015; BATCH-0011-E019; BATCH-0028-E016).","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0009-E003","BATCH-0015-E006","BATCH-0019-E006","BATCH-0005-E004","BATCH-0008-E014","BATCH-0018-E004"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0010-E015","BATCH-0011-E019","BATCH-0028-E016","BATCH-0011-E002","BATCH-0016-E008"],"limitations_and_gaps":["The evidence identifies appointments but rarely measures appointee capability or subsequent performance.","Several relevant appointments predate or postdate the target year, limiting direct period fit."]},{"question_id":"8B.5","answer":"Coordination mechanisms existed and achieved some territorial and institutional reach, but coordination and compliance were inconsistent. The CPVS monitored presidential commitments, the governors’ conference linked central and provincial governments, and security meetings sought joint implementation across FARDC, MONUSCO, EAC, ministries, and provincial authorities (BATCH-0020-E014; BATCH-0006-E007; BATCH-0021-E001). PDL-145T reached planned activity across dozens of territories and agencies, with hundreds of works reported ready or underway (BATCH-0023-E001; BATCH-0019-E009). Conversely, election administration suffered delayed openings, extended voting, procedural deviations, incomplete audit transparency, and major logistical failures (BATCH-0001-E016; BATCH-0007-E011; BATCH-0013-E008), while development monitoring among implementing agencies was poorly aligned and only half of Joint Resilience Programme activities were fully implemented (BATCH-0002-E001; BATCH-0002-E004).","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0020-E014","BATCH-0006-E007","BATCH-0021-E001","BATCH-0023-E001","BATCH-0019-E009"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0001-E016","BATCH-0007-E011","BATCH-0013-E008","BATCH-0002-E001","BATCH-0002-E004","BATCH-0011-E005"],"limitations_and_gaps":["The index contains few systematic ministry-by-ministry compliance or milestone datasets.","Some coordination evidence is official reporting without independent verification."]},{"question_id":"8B.6","answer":"Several priorities became observable practice rather than remaining slogans. Free primary education was implemented and associated with a large increase in public-primary enrollment, although quality and equity remained uncertain (BATCH-0014-E004; BATCH-0012-R01-E019); PDL-145T entered construction and procurement with reported schools, health centers, administrative buildings, roads, and local monitoring arrangements (BATCH-0023-E001; BATCH-0023-E002; BATCH-0010-E010); and justice, anti-trafficking, victim-reparation, fiscal, mining, and anti-money-laundering laws and institutions were enacted or staffed (BATCH-0009-E004; BATCH-0019-E003; BATCH-0029-E001; BATCH-0029-E003). Yet execution was partial: free maternity care and universal health coverage remained in implementation, budget execution was imperfect, later reviews identified incoherent spending and works without observed field action, and the election process displayed severe operational failures (BATCH-0020-E012; BATCH-0022-E008; BATCH-0024-E003; BATCH-0019-E013).","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0014-E004","BATCH-0012-R01-E019","BATCH-0023-E001","BATCH-0023-E002","BATCH-0010-E010","BATCH-0009-E004","BATCH-0019-E003","BATCH-0029-E001","BATCH-0029-E003"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0020-E012","BATCH-0022-E008","BATCH-0024-E003","BATCH-0019-E013","BATCH-0002-E001","BATCH-0013-E004"],"limitations_and_gaps":["Many service and infrastructure results are government-reported or donor-supported.","The index does not provide comprehensive national completion, quality, enforcement, or distribution data."]},{"question_id":"8B.7","answer":"Progress toward the program was mixed and attribution-sensitive. Education enrollment and some PDL-145T works moved in the intended direction, and 2023 fiscal execution was high in aggregate, but free education’s quality and reach remained uneven (BATCH-0014-E004; BATCH-0019-E009; BATCH-0024-E002; BATCH-0022-E010). Macroeconomic growth was reported at 6.2% while inflation reached 33.9% at year end and the franc depreciated substantially, so improved output did not clearly translate into purchasing-power gains (BATCH-0022-E004; BATCH-0022-E008; BATCH-0010-E003). Security goals substantially receded: M23 retained or expanded territory, displacement reached roughly 6.8–6.9 million, and violence and food insecurity remained severe, although armed-group action, regional intervention, inherited fragility, and external shocks limit presidential causal attribution (BATCH-0006-E002; BATCH-0013-E014; BATCH-0010-E003; BATCH-0020-E009).","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0014-E004","BATCH-0019-E009","BATCH-0024-E002","BATCH-0022-E004"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0022-E008","BATCH-0010-E003","BATCH-0006-E002","BATCH-0013-E014","BATCH-0020-E009","BATCH-0027-E006"],"limitations_and_gaps":["Most outcome series are national or multi-year and do not isolate 2023 presidential effects.","Security and welfare outcomes are heavily confounded by armed groups, neighboring states, donor resources, conflict displacement, and inherited conditions."]},{"question_id":"8B.8","answer":"There is credible evidence of some monitoring and adaptation, but correction was incomplete. Tshisekedi created and chaired the CPVS, approved a 2023 roadmap, reviewed implementation difficulties, and set milestones for PDL-145T and social commitments (BATCH-0020-E011; BATCH-0020-E012; BATCH-0020-E014). He convened a national roundtable to reassess the state of siege and later announced gradual easing, and the government ended the EAC force mandate after judging that it had not achieved expected results (BATCH-0021-E012; BATCH-0008-E007; BATCH-0011-E016). Ministers and agencies also conducted education, judicial, and electoral reviews, including audits and performance meetings (BATCH-0023-E006; BATCH-0023-E015; BATCH-0027-E011). However, evidence of corrective implementation is weak: the state of siege remained associated with worsening violence and abuses, election-audit recommendations were not shown to be acted upon, justice and corruption failures persisted, and monitoring systems were poorly coordinated (BATCH-0012-R03-E004; BATCH-0013-E009; BATCH-0028-E001; BATCH-0002-E004).","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0020-E011","BATCH-0020-E012","BATCH-0020-E014","BATCH-0021-E012","BATCH-0008-E007","BATCH-0011-E016","BATCH-0023-E006","BATCH-0023-E015"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0012-R03-E004","BATCH-0013-E009","BATCH-0028-E001","BATCH-0002-E004","BATCH-0017-E002","BATCH-0024-E004"],"limitations_and_gaps":["The index often records reviews, recommendations, or announced corrections without confirming completion.","It does not consistently distinguish presidential learning from ministerial or donor-led adaptation."]},{"question_id":"8B.9","answer":"Tshisekedi maintained active crisis-management and diplomatic decision-making, but results were mixed and sometimes counterproductive to stated objectives. He convened security and regional meetings, pursued Nairobi, Luanda, EAC, MONUSCO, Uganda, AU, UN, and ICC channels, requested sanctions and accountability, and later replaced or ended regional arrangements judged ineffective (BATCH-0021-E001; BATCH-0021-E006; BATCH-0019-E001; BATCH-0011-E016). He also ordered or supported election scheduling, monetary measures, PDL-145T coordination, and a gradual easing review of the state of siege (BATCH-0007-E008; BATCH-0024-E005; BATCH-0021-E012). Adverse evidence is substantial: M23 remained territorially powerful, displacement and violence increased, the EAC strategy failed to deliver expected security gains, and security forces violently suppressed opposition and Wazalendo protests while authorities restricted media and political activity (BATCH-0011-E017; BATCH-0013-E014; BATCH-0011-E018; BATCH-0028-E015). Some failures reflect armed-group, regional, and international constraints rather than direct presidential control.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0021-E001","BATCH-0021-E006","BATCH-0019-E001","BATCH-0011-E016","BATCH-0007-E008","BATCH-0024-E005","BATCH-0021-E012"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0011-E017","BATCH-0013-E014","BATCH-0011-E018","BATCH-0028-E015","BATCH-0010-E012","BATCH-0019-E012"],"limitations_and_gaps":["The index cannot establish the president’s personal command responsibility for every subordinate security action.","Diplomatic and military outcomes are affected by Rwanda, M23, other armed groups, regional forces, MONUSCO, and external shocks."]},{"question_id":"8B.10","answer":"By the end of 2023, Tshisekedi had converted meaningful portions of his program into durable or partially durable law, institutions, administrative practice, and some service delivery, but not into broad, securely attributable goal achievement. Durable advances included the statutory and institutional framework for free education, victim reparations, justice staffing, anti-money-laundering, fiscal governance, PDL-145T implementation machinery, and continuing health and education programs (BATCH-0012-R01-E019; BATCH-0029-E001; BATCH-0009-E004; BATCH-0019-E003; BATCH-0029-E003; BATCH-0010-E004). The government also completed the constitutional election timetable and retained executive and coalition control, though the process was heavily disputed and operationally defective (BATCH-0010-E005; BATCH-0028-E010; BATCH-0013-E008). Against this, security objectives were not achieved: the state of siege failed to restore security, M23 and other armed groups remained active, displacement and food insecurity were extreme, and institutional reforms remained fragile or donor-dependent (BATCH-0012-R03-E004; BATCH-0011-E016; BATCH-0013-E014; BATCH-0020-E009; BATCH-0014-E003). The end-period record therefore shows real institutional conversion and partial delivery alongside major reversals, weak durability, and substantial causal uncertainty.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0012-R01-E019","BATCH-0029-E001","BATCH-0009-E004","BATCH-0019-E003","BATCH-0029-E003","BATCH-0010-E004","BATCH-0010-E005","BATCH-0028-E010"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0012-R03-E004","BATCH-0011-E016","BATCH-0013-E014","BATCH-0020-E009","BATCH-0014-E003","BATCH-0028-E018","BATCH-0013-E010"],"limitations_and_gaps":["The period is short for judging long-term durability, especially for health care, infrastructure, and institutional reforms begun during 2023.","Independent evidence of outcomes and ruler-specific causation is much stronger for security and election failures than for positive service delivery."]}],"cross_lens_observations":["The evidence supports a mostly explicit and substantially operationalized program, but implementation and outcomes were uneven across domains.","Development, education, fiscal, judicial, and monitoring machinery show real administrative conversion; security, electoral integrity, justice, and corruption records show major execution gaps.","Attribution is strongest for presidential statements, appointments, ordinances, CPVS direction, and high-level crisis choices, and weaker for subordinate implementation, donor-supported services, electoral administration, and conflict outcomes.","Moral approval or disapproval of Tshisekedi’s objectives is not used in these answers; the analysis concerns clarity, execution, adaptation, control, and attributable progress only."]}
